slides.title: Power cut over a **theft** bill?
slides.subtitle: If the bill looks **arbitrary**, the High Court can order supply restored on a deposit of at least **50%**.

slides.label: The case
slides.title: A **Rs 93 lakh** theft bill
bullets: A Gujarat business was accused of electricity theft and billed about **₹93 lakh**, plus about **₹23 lakh** as compounding charges.
The Gujarat High Court let it deposit **50%** of the bill and ordered the power to be **reconnected**.
The power companies appealed. Justices **Manoj Misra** and **K.V. Viswanathan** dismissed their appeal.

slides.label: What the court said
slides.title: Theft bills follow **Section 126**
bullets: There is no separate procedure for theft. The bill must follow **Section 126**, Electricity Act: provisional bill, **objections**, **hearing**, then final bill.
The final assessment can be challenged in **appeal under Section 127**, after depositing **half** the assessed amount.
Restoring supply is an **emergency** remedy, because electricity is essential for life and livelihood.
slides.note: **Law fact:** If a criminal case follows, the **Special Court** decides final liability, and any excess deposit must be **refunded**.

slides.label: Keep in mind
slides.title: **50%** is not an automatic right
bullets: Theft involves **criminal intent**, so High Courts must be **careful** in such cases.
The 50% route is for a provisional bill that looks **prima facie arbitrary**, and the court must record **reasons**.
In a suitable case, the High Court can still ask for the **full** provisional amount first.

slides.label: If you get a theft bill
slides.title: Use the **remedies** the law gives
bullets: File your **objections** to the provisional assessment and take part in the **hearing**.
If the final bill is still wrong, you can file an **appeal under Section 127**.

caption:
Accused of electricity theft and your power was cut? The Supreme Court has explained your remedies ⚡⚖️

A Gujarat business was accused of electricity theft and billed about ₹93 lakh, plus about ₹23 lakh in compounding charges. The Gujarat High Court allowed it to deposit 50% of the bill and get its power reconnected. The power companies challenged this, and the Supreme Court dismissed their appeal.

The Court held that there is no separate procedure for theft bills. They must follow Section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003: a provisional assessment, a chance to file objections, a hearing, and then a final assessment. The final assessment can be appealed under Section 127, which needs a deposit of half the assessed amount. If a criminal case follows, the Special Court decides final liability, and any excess deposit must be refunded.

But 50% is not an automatic right. Because theft involves criminal intent, High Courts must be careful. Where the provisional bill looks prima facie arbitrary, the High Court may, for recorded reasons, order supply restored on a deposit of at least 50%. In a suitable case, it can still ask for the full provisional amount.

Case: Dakshin Gujarat Vij Company Ltd. v. Vaibhav Metal Crusher, 2026 INSC 1157 (Supreme Court, Justices Manoj Misra and K.V. Viswanathan)
